title: Famous People and Heroes

parts.title: My hero
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When people ask me who my hero is, they expect me to name a singer or a footballer. In fact, it is my grandmother. She is not famous, and she has never been on television, but she is the bravest person I know.

My grandmother grew up in a small village with no electricity. When she was fourteen, her father became ill, and she had to leave school to work on the family farm. She got up at four every morning to feed the animals, and she did this for twenty years.

Later, she moved to the city and opened a small shop, where she sold bread and cakes. At first, no one came in, but she kept going. She gave free cake to children after school, and soon their parents began to visit as well. After five years, the shop was the most popular in the street.

She always says, 'You can't change what happens to you, but you can choose what you do about it.' I think about those words whenever something goes wrong. When I am older, I hope that I can be as strong and as kind as she is.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about his hero?
options: She is a well-known singer in town
She appeared on television once or twice
She was a famous writer in the city
She is not famous but very brave
questions.explanation: She is not famous, but she is the bravest person he knows.

questions.prompt: Why did his grandmother leave school?
options: The school was too far away
She wanted to earn some money
The family moved to the city
questions.explanation: Her father became ill, so she had to work on the farm.

questions.prompt: How did she attract customers to her shop?
options: She put up bright new posters
She sold cheap bread to everyone
She gave free cake to children
questions.explanation: She gave free cake to children after school.

questions.prompt: What was the shop like after five years?
options: It was the most popular in the street
It was still quite empty then
It had to close for a short while
It had moved to a bigger street
questions.explanation: After five years, the shop was the most popular in the street.

questions.prompt: What does the writer hope for the future?
options: To open a shop of his own one day
To travel the world like her
To become a famous person like others
To be strong and kind like her
questions.explanation: He hopes to be as strong and kind as she is.

parts.title: A famous inventor
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Thomas Alva Edison is one of the most famous inventors in history. He was born in 1847 in the United States, and as a child he was always curious about how things worked. [1] His teacher thought he was slow, so his mother took him out of school and taught him at home.

Edison loved to experiment, and at the age of ten, he built a small laboratory in his cellar. [2] Sometimes, his experiments made so much smoke that his family was afraid.

As an adult, he invented many things, including a machine that could record sound. [3] He is probably best known for the electric light bulb, which he improved after trying thousands of materials.

When people asked him about his failures, he answered that he had found a thousand ways that did not work. [4] His strong will is the reason why he became so successful. [5] Today, many of his ideas are still used all over the world.
sentences: He asked so many questions that the other pupils got tired of him.
In the end, he held more than a thousand patents.
He was also very good at selling his ideas.
People could hardly believe that a machine could repeat a voice.
He sold newspapers and sweets on trains when he was twelve.
They were so surprised that they gave him a prize.
Few people have changed the way we live as much as he did.
He spent all his pocket money on bottles and chemicals.

gaps.explanation: Asking so many questions explains why the teacher thought he was slow.
Spending money on bottles and chemicals goes with the cellar laboratory and smoke.
The machine that could record sound surprised people: they could hardly believe it could repeat a voice.
He held over a thousand patents, which supports his determination.
Few people changed life as much leads to many ideas still being used today.

parts.title: An email about a concert
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Jon, You will never guess what happened! I [1] a ticket for the concert of my favourite singer. She is performing here [2] Saturday, and I have never seen her live. Tickets [3] sold out in less than an hour, so I was very lucky. I [4] to take my sister, but she is on holiday. Would you [5] to come with me? The show starts at eight, [6] we should leave at six.

questions.prompt: Gap 2

questions.prompt: Gap 3

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Past simple "wanted to take".

questions.prompt: Gap 5

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: "So" shows the result.

parts.title: Heroes of everyday life
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: When we think of heroes, we often imagine soldiers or film stars, but real heroes are all around us. Teachers who stay late to help a child, nurses who work through the night, and neighbours who give food to people in need are all heroes. They do not do these things to become famous, [1] because they care. One woman, who lives in my street, collects clothes [2] families who have lost their homes. She has been doing it for ten years, and she never asks for thanks. Heroes like her teach us that even small acts can make a big difference. [3] you ever feel you are too young or too busy to help, remember that kindness costs nothing. Why not start today? You can help [4] person who needs it, and you will feel proud of [5] you have done. Everybody [6] be a hero in their own way.

gaps.explanation: "Not to become famous, but because they care".

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Science Centre. A short message about today’s programme. The new space show was going to start at ten, as it says on our leaflet, but the machine in the dome needs a repair, so please ignore that time. We will open the doors at the start of the lunch hour, at twelve, just after the café has put out the sandwiches. There is also a later show at two, but it is only for school groups. Tickets are free, and you can collect one at the desk by the main door. Thank you for your patience.

question.prompt: When does the new show start?
question.explanation: The leaflet says ten but the machine needs a repair, and the show at two is only for school groups; the doors open at twelve, at the start of the lunch hour, so the show starts at noon.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Who’s the man in the big painting, Niall? He looks very important.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I thought it might be the painter at first, because there’s a name at the bottom. But that’s the signature of the artist, and it’s a woman called Helen Brown.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh, I see. Is he a doctor then? He’s holding a book.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s what I said to my sister, but look at the sign on the wall. It says he ruled the country for forty years, and he’s wearing a crown on his head.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Of course! I didn’t notice the crown.

question.prompt: Who is the man in the painting?
question.explanation: Niall says the name is the artist’s signature, not the man’s, and the doctor idea is wrong; the sign says he ruled the country and he wears a crown, so he is a king.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi Gideon, it’s Cecilia. I finished the book you lent me, and I wanted to tell you at once. You said that the first chapters were slow, and I almost stopped reading on page twenty, but I’m glad I didn’t, because after that I couldn’t put it down. It’s about six hundred pages, but I read it in a week and it never felt heavy. The last pages were the hardest. I was on the train and I had tears in my eyes. Call me back when you can, and we’ll talk about it.

question.prompt: What does the woman say about the book?
options: The first part is quite boring
question.explanation: The beginning was slow but she kept reading, and the length did not bother her; the end made her cry on the train, so the ending was sad.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you get your football signed, Stellan? Your brother said you waited for hours.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Well, I took a magazine with a big photo of him on the cover, and I was ready to give it to him, but there were hundreds of people and he couldn’t reach it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: What about the ball? I thought you were going to bring one.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I left it at home, I’m afraid. In the end a boy next to me was wearing his team shirt, and the player smiled and signed that. I was a bit jealous, but it was nice to watch.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Poor you!

question.explanation: Stellan did not give the magazine and left his ball at home; the player signed the shirt that a boy was wearing.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Why do you like your new teacher so much, Oriel? You always talk about her.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Well, people say she’s funny, and she does tell good stories sometimes, but that’s not why. She doesn’t give much homework either, only a little, and that’s nice.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So what is it, then?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Last week my friend Jack was failing maths. Other teachers had stopped trying, but she stayed with him after school every day until he understood it. She’s still doing it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s really kind of her.

question.prompt: Why does the girl admire her teacher?
options: She never gives up on pupils
question.explanation: Oriel says the teacher is funny and gives little homework, but admires her because she stayed with Jack every day when other teachers gave up.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Welcome to Film Hour. This week I saw a new film that I want to tell you about. A lot of people expect it to be about a soldier who later becomes a king, because of the poster with a crown and a sword, but that’s only a small part of the story. And there is a teacher in a village, who appears for five minutes at the beginning. The real heart of the film is a young nurse who works in a tent near the battlefield and helps hurt soldiers get home. It made me think. Go and see it.

options: A soldier who later became a king
A teacher in a small village
question.explanation: The soldier and the teacher are only small parts; the film is really about a young nurse who looks after hurt soldiers.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Ursula, you have a lovely accent. Where are you from? The capital?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Everybody asks me that. My parents lived there when they married, and later we moved to a village high up in the mountains when I was six, but I was born before that.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So where, then?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: In the same place where my grandfather kept his fishing boat. You can see the sea from the main street, and the whole town smells of salt in the morning.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That sounds lovely.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It is. I go back every summer.

question.explanation: The family lived in the capital and moved to the mountains later, but she was born near where her grandfather kept his fishing boat, a town by the sea.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Well, that was a long morning. I’m tired. Did you enjoy the charity race, Vaughan?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I did. People said it was too long, but I don’t mind that when it’s for a good reason.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: True. The prizes were quite small, weren’t they? Just a box of chocolates.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I didn’t mind that either. What I liked were the helpers. They gave out water, they cheered for everyone, and they stayed until the very last runner.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I know! They were so friendly. I’d like to thank them.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Let’s write a message on the club website tonight.

question.prompt: What do Polly and Vaughan agree about?
options: The helpers did a great job
question.explanation: They both accept the long distance and the small prizes, and they praise the helpers who gave water, cheered and stayed to the end.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I heard you are learning the guitar, Kiri. Are you starting a band with your brother?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No, he’s much better than I am. I’d be embarrassed. He did ask me once, but I said no.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Is it for the trip to Spain? You’ll hear a lot of guitar music there.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Not really. We leave in March and I won’t be good by then. It’s for me. My job is stressful, and when I get home I need something that clears my head. Ten minutes of music helps me feel peaceful.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s a good idea. I might try it too.

question.prompt: Why is Kiri going to learn the guitar?
question.explanation: She says her brother asked her to play and the trip is too soon, but she wants something that clears her head after a stressful job.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Aldo, I saw a house in the country for sale. It has a big garden and a stream. Would you like to move?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: The price is quite good, so that’s not a problem. And I’m not worried about feeling alone, I’d make friends quickly.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So what’s stopping you?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Nothing really. Our kids spend all day with their phones in the flat. In the country they could play outside, climb trees, and learn about animals. I think they would be happier and healthier.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You’re right. Shall we go and see it on Sunday?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes, let’s book a visit.

question.prompt: What does Aldo think about the idea of moving to the country?
options: It would be good for the children
question.explanation: He says the price is fine and he would not be lonely; the main thing is that the children would play outside, so he thinks it would be good for them.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are you excited about the school play, Janet? I heard you have a big part.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: A bit, yes, but I’ve learned all my words already, so that’s fine. I’m not frightened of the audience, because my parents will be there and they always make me feel safe.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So is it going well?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Honestly, we have practice every evening this week and it’s the same scenes again and again. I wish it were over. I’d rather be at home with a book.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I understand. It’ll be worth it on Friday.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I hope so.

question.prompt: How does Janet feel about the school play?
question.explanation: She has learned her words and is not afraid of the audience, but the repeated evening practice makes her tired of it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Vance, are we still having the party on Saturday? I’ve told everybody.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Actually, I wanted to ask you about that. Could we move it to Sunday? Our friend Marco is flying home on Saturday night, and it wouldn’t be the same without him.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I checked the weather, and it says rain on Sunday. And the hall is booked for both days.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hmm. We can use the garden if it doesn’t rain, and if it does, we can move into the kitchen. I want Marco there.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Fine, I’ll call everyone this evening.

question.prompt: Why does Vance suggest changing the date of the party?
question.explanation: Eliza mentions rain and the hall, but Vance says those are not problems; he wants his friend Marco to be at the party.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So, Sienna, what are your new neighbours like?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Quiet, which is nice. I thought they’d be noisy, with three children, but I hardly hear them.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are they friendly?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes. They brought me a cake on the first day, and they smile in the corridor. But when I invited them for tea, they went red and said they were busy. I think they just don’t know what to say to new people.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Maybe they’ll relax.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I hope so. I’ll keep inviting them.

question.prompt: How does Sienna feel about her new neighbours?
question.explanation: She says they are not noisy and brought a cake, but they went red and refused tea, so she thinks they are friendly and shy.

parts.title: A talk about a famous scientist
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for coming to the Harbour Museum open day. My name is Brenda, and I am one of the guides. I’d like to tell you about the day. First, the opening hours. The museum is open from nine in the morning, but today we are opening early, at half past eight, for the open day. The tickets are free today. Normally, an adult ticket costs twelve pounds, but you are paying nothing. The first tour begins in the entrance hall at ten o’clock. It lasts an hour, and we will see the old fishing boats. We thought about starting in the cellar, where the old maps are kept, but it was too cold. Then there is the workshop on the second floor, where children can make a small ship out of wood. Some people think that it is on the third floor, but that is the café. Please remember to wear old clothes, because the paint can be messy. After the workshop, at one o’clock, you can have lunch in the café. We have a special menu today. The most popular dish is fish soup, and if you do not like fish, there is also a cheese sandwich, but I always take the soup. For the afternoon, there is a talk by a retired sailor named Mr Hughes, at three o’clock. He sailed around the world twice, and he has a lot of stories. Some of the stories are about storms, but most of them are about the places he saw, and the people he met. At the end of the day, you can buy postcards at the shop. They cost one pound each. If you want a bigger souvenir, a model ship is ten pounds, but I think the postcards are nicer. Thank you, and enjoy your day.

gaps.prompt: The museum opens early at ___ for the open day
gaps.explanation: Normally it opens at nine, but today it opens at half past eight.

gaps.prompt: The first tour begins in the ___
gaps.explanation: The tour starts in the entrance hall; the cellar was too cold.

gaps.prompt: Children make a small ship out of wood in the ___ on the second floor
gaps.explanation: The workshop is on the second floor; the third floor is the café.

gaps.prompt: The most popular dish in the café is ___
gaps.explanation: The most popular dish is fish soup; the other choice is a cheese sandwich.

gaps.prompt: The speaker at three o'clock is a retired ___
gaps.explanation: Mr Hughes is a retired sailor who sailed around the world twice.
Postcards cost one pound each; a model ship is ten pounds.

parts.title: A famous author
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: Mirela, welcome to the programme. Your books are everywhere. Who was the first person to read your stories?

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: Oh, you’d think it was my parents, wouldn’t you? But they were always busy with work, and I never showed them anything. I wrote my first story for my little brother, who was seven at the time. He would sit on the end of my bed and listen to every chapter, and he always told me what he thought, even when it was not kind. I still call him before I send a book to my publisher.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: Where do your ideas come from?

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: People imagine it must be from my own childhood, but that was actually quite ordinary. And I don’t borrow ideas from other books, I try not to. Mostly I listen. I sit on a bus or in a park and I hear a few words from a stranger, or I watch someone’s face, and a whole story begins in my head.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: How do you feel about being famous?

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: Delighted would be the wrong word. I’m happy that people enjoy my work, of course, and I don’t mind the readers at all, they are lovely. But I’m shy by nature, so when someone recognises me in a shop I go red and forget what to say. It still feels a little strange to me.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: Where do you write?

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: I used to write in the town library, because it was quiet, and I tried my bedroom for a while, but there is a bed there and I fall asleep. Now I go every morning to a small café near my house. The people there know me, and nobody asks any questions. I order a coffee, and I work for four hours.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: What advice would you give to young writers?

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: Don’t wait until midnight to write, like in the films, you’ll just be tired. And you needn’t show your work to famous authors, they’re busy people. My advice is to read as much as you can, and to keep every page you write, even the bad ones, because one day you may use them.

turns.speaker: lucian
turns.text: Tell us about your new book.

turns.speaker: mirela
turns.text: It isn’t about the sea, although I did go on a boat for research and I was sick the whole time. And it’s not about a school either, I’ve done that already. It’s a mystery that happens in an old lighthouse, with a keeper who disappears on a stormy night. I won’t tell you more.

questions.prompt: Who was Mirela's first reader?
questions.explanation: She says she never showed her parents anything and wrote her first story for her little brother, who listened to every chapter.

questions.prompt: Where do her ideas come from?
options: From things she sees and hears
questions.explanation: Her childhood was ordinary and she tries not to borrow from books; she listens to strangers and watches faces.

questions.prompt: How does she feel about being famous?
options: A bit strange because she is shy
questions.explanation: She is happy that people enjoy her books but she is shy, so being recognised feels strange.

questions.prompt: Where does she write?
options: In a library in the town
At a desk in her bedroom
In a café near her home
questions.explanation: She used to write in the library and tried her bedroom but fell asleep; now she works every morning in a café near her house.

questions.prompt: What advice does she give?
options: Read a lot and keep everything
Show your work to famous authors
questions.explanation: She says do not write at midnight and do not show work to famous authors; read a lot and keep every page.

questions.prompt: What is her new book about?
questions.explanation: The book is not about the sea or a school; it is a mystery in an old lighthouse.
